A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RoPECraft, with matching methods and original experiments. Text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable; v1 Appendices A.1–A.5 are retained, and v2 adds A.6.

before.justification: v1 reports original DAVIS motion-transfer experiments, quantitative comparisons in Tables 1–3, and qualitative component and Fourier-feature ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains the original experimental results and adds runtime measurements, a human preference study and RealCamVid evaluation.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and Sections 4.1–4.3 retain the same optical-flow-based RoPE warping, early-step flow-matching optimization and Fourier phase regularization. The added evaluations do not introduce a method component or alter the procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on a RealCamVid subset containing camera motion and multiple objects, alongside the retained DAVIS evaluation (Appendix A.6, Table 6 and Figure 13). This materially broadens the tested scene distribution; the new user study itself reuses DAVIS.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator set remains GWTF, SMM, MOFT, ConMo and both DiTFlow variants. The runtime, user-study and RealCamVid comparisons use these existing methods; DF-L and DF-R in Table 5 denote the retained DiTFlow variants.

E3.justification: Section 5.5 introduces a two-part human evaluation using 20 randomly sampled DAVIS prompt-reference pairs, with top-three selections for motion matching and visual preference. v2 also adds runtime evaluation and random RealCamVid subsampling. The original backbone choices, optimization settings and 50-step generation budget remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands validation of the motion metric through controlled magnitude/offset examples in Figure 9 and comparison with human motion judgments in Table 4. Figure 13 also adds challenging camera-motion and multiple-subject cases. The existing component, optimization-budget and Fourier-feature ablations are retained.

E5.justification: Table 1's uncertainty reporting and the identical-seed controls in Figures 6–7 remain unchanged. New runtime results extend the existing plus/minus reporting style, without specifying a new estimation procedure, repeated-run count, confidence interval or significance test. The user-study percentages have no reported uncertainty.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their values, but substantial new results appear. On RealCamVid, RoPECraft leads Table 6 with MF 0.7019, CLIP 0.2141 and FTD 0.1697. Table 5 reports 30% first-choice preference versus 19% for the strongest baseline, MOFT. v2 also adds metric-alignment percentages, toy-example scores, qualitative examples and runtime measurements.

T1.justification: The flow-matching and RoPE mathematics, discrete Fréchet definition, FTD aggregation and Fourier losses are unchanged. Figure 9 illustrates previously stated metric behavior without introducing a new formal definition, assumption, derivation or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list and conclusion retain the same substantive claims about training-free RoPE-based motion transfer and the proposed FTD metric. The additions supply supporting evaluation without redefining the core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 expands the explanation of MF's insensitivity to magnitude and spatial offset, interprets the user study as supporting FTD's perceptual alignment, and presents the timings as an efficiency-quality tradeoff. Appendix A.6 adds a robustness interpretation for complex scenes. The existing limitations in A.5 remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 5.4 newly discloses per-method execution times, including 109.231 ± 3.112 seconds for RoPECraft, adding computational-cost information. Existing hyperparameters, hardware, prompt-generation instructions, FTD pseudocode and project access information are retained; the timing measurement procedure is not specified.

R1.justification: v2 adds the RealCam-Vid dataset paper as reference 49 to support the new evaluation. The related-work discussion and positioning relative to GWTF and DiTFlow remain unchanged; Open-Sora's shift from reference 49 to 50 is only renumbering.

P1.justification: The revision adds Sections 5.5 and A.6 and expands the metric and quantitative-results explanations while preserving the existing narrative and method text. Affiliations, correspondence information and the conference footer are also updated.

P2.justification: v2 adds the metric illustration in Figure 9, user-study Tables 4–5, RealCamVid Table 6 and qualitative Figure 13. Existing figures and tables are preserved, with renumbering and localized reflow of the results pages rather than a wholesale visual redesign.

improvement.justification: The user study, RealCamVid evaluation and runtime measurements add useful evidence about perceptual relevance, generalization and computational cost that v1 lacked. Their contribution is limited by the unspecified participant count, RealCamVid subset size and timing procedure. These additions modestly strengthen the paper while leaving its method and original results unchanged.
